prize_parts.citation: for showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reshape international trade, so that gains from trade arise through reallocation across firms as well as across industries

statement.case_for: I keep B034 first after reading the openings. The contribution is a change in how a whole field models its object. Before Melitz (2003), trade models used representative firms, and gains from trade came mainly from specialisation across industries. Afterwards, selection, exporter premia and within-industry reallocation became standard channels. The idea has spread into macroeconomics, productivity measurement and industrial organisation. More than twenty years of replication and use mean the maturity test is met without qualification, which is not true of every strong candidate on the shortlist. Attribution is also fairly tight. Melitz's 2003 model is the anchor. Helpman's work with Melitz and Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, and his earlier work on monopolistic competition and trade, gives the lineage and the empirical bridge. A two-person award matches that structure. Colleagues rank it high across very different fields, with six top-three placements. That is not merit evidence in itself, but the written assessments, including those from members who ranked it lower, do not dispute the core contribution or its maturity.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is thematic and attributional. The 2008 prize recognised new trade theory, so some members may see heterogeneous-firm models as a refinement rather than a new field. Credit is also contested outside this ballot's names. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made closely related empirical and quantitative contributions, and Yeaple is part of the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple strand. A two-name award leaves out credible contributors. The size of the welfare gains also depends on model structure and parametrisation.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B034 second but warns that the committee may regard Krugman's 2008 prize as covering the territory. He also flags unresolved priority questions involving Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum, and notes that Helpman appears on another trade entry.
responses.response: I take the 2008 overlap seriously, but I would separate the two contributions. Krugman explained trade between similar countries and the role of scale and variety. Melitz changed the unit of analysis from industry to firm and added selection, which gives a different mechanism for welfare gains. The priority question is real, and I cannot resolve it from the evidence here. Even so, the Bernard et al. work is largely empirical and quantitative, so it is not a clear competing claim to the selection model itself. That is why a Helpman-Melitz citation worded around selection and reallocation is defensible. I agree it should be worded narrowly. I also agree with the point about Helpman's political-economy entry. It does not weaken the case for the firm-heterogeneity work, and the citation should avoid implying a broader lifetime recognition.

responses.point: Teorell places B034 sixth and would add Redding as a third laureate. He also notes that Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are omitted and that the gains-from-trade implications depend on model structure.
responses.response: I agree the welfare implications are structure-dependent, and that is a real limit on how strongly the citation should speak about the size of gains. I would still resist adding Redding. His quantitative spatial and trade work is substantial, but it builds on the framework and is arguably a separate achievement with its own maturity clock. Including him would blur a clean attribution into a broad trade-and-quantification prize. Your Bernard et al. point is the stronger reservation, and I treat it as an open question rather than answering it. I would still choose a smaller, defensible credited set over one that tries to cover the whole literature.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B036 first and argues it pairs a clear framework with credible quasi-experimental evidence. She notes that omitting Dorn from an Autor-Katz-Hanson trio is a real cost and that the China-shock findings have held up.
responses.response: I agree B036 is an empirically careful programme, and I ranked it third. If the Committee goes that way, I would choose the Autor-Dorn-Hanson trio over adding Katz, because the trade-shock evidence is jointly authored and Dorn's omission would be hard to justify. Your point on robustness is fair, but I read the record as more mixed than 'held up'. Exposure measures, persistence and the role of automation remain debated. The task framework also overlaps conceptually with work already recognised in 2024, and Dreber and Stromberg raise the same credit problem. B034 is less exposed on both counts. It has no comparable dispute about magnitudes and no recent adjacent prize in the same lineage.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B047 first as a unified framework linking electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity to fiscal outcomes, with Persson, Tabellini and Besley as the natural trio.
responses.response: I rank B047 second and agree the attribution is cleaner than in most candidates. My reservation is the empirical side. Some constitutional-effects results rest on cross-country identification that is open to challenge. The 2024 institutions prize also makes the thematic overlap harder to dismiss than for trade. That is why B047 remains an alternative and not my preferred part. If the Committee finds the 2024 overlap manageable, I would not oppose it.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee treats heterogeneous-firm trade as a distinct advance over the 2008 new-trade-theory prize or as an extension of it.
How to weigh the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum and Yeaple contributions, which are outside the credited names, against a two-name credit.
Whether Redding belongs in the credit. I leave him out, but that rests on a judgement about maturity and distinctness that colleagues may reasonably reverse.
How far the welfare claims should be stated in a citation, given that gains-from-trade results depend on model structure and parametrisation.
I am relying on the supplied openings and my own reading of the literature, without independent verification of credit attributions.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My co-authors and institutional ties are in economic history and political science, with no listed link to Helpman, Melitz, Redding or the other shortlisted candidates. Lund ties to committee colleagues do not concern these candidates.
